item.title: How the ‘Zed Beats’ music movement give Zambians back their voice
item.description: This blend of indigenous musical elements with international influences uses local languages, which has great resonance with young people.
item.content:encoded:
Zed Beats is a music movement that evolved in the late 1980s when young producers started using computers to blend western music with local languages and flavour. Today it’s an umbrella term for popular urban music in Zambia.

Musician and academic Mathew Tembo is a Zed Beats specialist. His PhD is on its history, production and musical labour from 1986 to 2024. We asked him to tell us about the music and how it shapes the country.

What is Zed Beats?

Zed Beats takes its name from the “Z” in “Zambia”. It’s a blend of indigenous musical elements with influences drawn from R&B, reggae, rap, Jamaican dancehall, hip-hop, Afrobeats, amapiano and other urban music genres trending at the time of its production.

The music, sung mostly in Zambian languages Chinyanja and Chibemba, along with some English, is produced on digital audio workstations by self-taught producers in home studios. The use of local languages makes Zed Beats resonate with young people, whose everyday conversations are carried out in these languages.

What forces created the ‘new’ music?

item.title: Geetanjali Shree’s radical fiction, written in Hindi, is finding a global audience
item.description: Shree has explored the postcolonial tension between Hindi and English with piercing acuity in her five collections of short stories and five novels.
item.content:encoded:
In 2022, Tomb of Sand became the first work of Indian literature to win the International Booker Prize. Written in Hindi by Geetanjali Shree and translated by Daisy Rockwell, the novel is Shree’s magnum opus and the pinnacle of a distinguished literary career.

Indian writers have previously won the Booker Prize, which is restricted to works written in English: Salman Rushdie (1981), Arundhati Roy (1997), Kiran Desai (2006) and Aravind Adiga (2008). But English is spoken by about 10% of the Indian population; its rightful place as an Indian language is a result of the passionately contested legacy of 200 years of British rule on the subcontinent.

Hindustani – or Hindi, as it is commonly known – has 611 million speakers around the world. Some estimates put the figure closer to 855 million. And yet the global recognition of Hindi literature, like literature in the 22 other officially recognised languages of India, each of which has its own complex history, remains hostage to Anglophone publishing regimes.

Shree notes this conundrum in one of her earliest stories, Pilaki Mane Faye (the title is a bit of nonsensical wordplay, implying the absurdity of a situation). item.title: Mumbai’s chawl residents negotiate with ‘light mafias’ for power supply
item.description: Informal settlements are forced to rely on illegal operators who provide low-voltage, irregular electricity which is risky and expensive.
item.content:encoded:
“We pay Rs 600 every month whether we get electricity or not. We used to pay more but there are now two electricity mafias competing in this area,” says Ajuma Sheikh, a 63-year-old social worker who stays in Patra chawl in Mumbai’s Mankhurd suburb.

For the past 25 years, she has been caught between the powerful stakeholders of Mumbai’s electricity sector: the government, Adani Electricity and local unauthorised operators.

In and around the Mumbai Port Trust, reserve forest areas and on land owned by the Railways and Defence departments, thousands of people live like the residents of Patra chawl – in densely-packed, make-shift homes made of tin sheets and plastic tarp with poor ventilation and no reliable electricity.

“We sit outside all day because it’s too hot to go in,” Sheikh says, pointing to clusters of plastic chairs, cardboard sheets, cement bags, wooden planks, and ripped mattresses arranged haphazardly along the Mankhurd railway track. “We go indoors at 2 am but get bit by mosquitoes all night. We can’t put up a net or light a coil because there’s no ventilation. We’ll suffocate.”

item.title: Bangladesh says PM Tarique Rahman will not visit India until Sheikh Hasina is extradited
item.description: The former prime minister’s ‘open media interactions’ ‘vitiated’ the possibility of Rahman’s visit, a Dhaka official said.
item.content:encoded:
Bangladesh said on Sunday that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would not visit India until New Delhi extradited former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, AFP reported.

The neighbouring countries have had strained relations since massive student-led protests erupted in Bangladesh in July 2024 against a controversial quota scheme for government jobs and later snowballed into a broader agitation against Hasina’s government. Her government was eventually brought down, forcing her to flee to India.

Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal in November sentenced Hasina to death for crimes against humanity in connection with the deadly crackdown on protesters in 2024. In February, a court sentenced her to 10 years’ imprisonment in two corruption cases relating to alleged irregularities in the allocation of land in a government housing project in Dhaka.

Dhaka has repeatedly demanded that Hasina be extradited. It has also expressed concerns about the ousted leader being allowed by the Indian authorities to address her supporters from Delhi.

New Delhi has previously said that it was for Hasina to decide whether she wants to return to Bangladesh.

Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Bangladesh’s foreign ministry official AKM Shahidul Karim played down media speculation about a possible trip by Rahman to India next week.

“We are of the view that a propitious environment needs to be created for the visit,” AFP quoted him as saying....

item.title: AI is flooding the online book market with poor translations: Here’s how to spot them
item.description: AI translations push the crafted work of real translators – with qualifications, genuine language skills, experience – to the back of a very busy marketplace.
item.content:encoded:
If you’re buying literature in translation online, buyer beware. You may unknowingly be buying low-quality AI-assisted translations presented as the work of a professional.

Certain online retailers are being used to flood the book market with AI-assisted “translations”. Amazon is one such example, though the company seems to be aware of the problem and claims to be addressing it.

I’m a published translator of French and Belgian literature and I teach literary translation to MA students. So I know from experience how much time and effort go into translation. Like many translators, I’m wary of the impact of AI on translation quality, not least because AI is not ideologically neutral. This means AI translation is more likely to reproduce outdated racial stereotypes (rife in colonial-era literature, alas) rather than handle them with sensitivity.

I first became aware of the practice when I purchased a Jules Verne novel in English online. The book presents as the work of a human translator and styles itself as “for a modern readership”. Within three minutes of opening the book, I had got my money back. Why? Style-wise, there was nothing “modern” about the “translation” – the style was as archaic as the first translation in 1877. item.title: ‘Attention and Drift’: A new vantage from which to look at literature and politics simultaneously
item.description: Author Prasanta Chakravarty studies the ideas of American philosophers George Santayana and Stanley Cavell.
item.content:encoded:
Prasanta Chakravarty’s Attention and Drift: Santayana and Cavell in the Present is an exuberant addition to what is already a versatile and impressive oeuvre. Chakravarty’s doctoral work was on the literature of the English Civil War of the 17th century. Since then, without losing his footing in the earlier centuries, he has engaged with themes unto the very present.

What unites his books is perhaps the ability to read literature and politics always simultaneously, each informing the other, each irreducible to the other. Thus, later works, including several edited ones, engage with figures like Machiavelli (in his historical period, as well as the shadow he casts today), as well as the complex thematics of what the media calls “populism”. Beyond this, he also edits a web journal, and is the author of four volumes of poetry.

Embracing risk and danger

The latest book on attention and drift is a study of two influential philosophers who are not generally paired together – George Santayana (1863-1952) and Stanley Cavell (1926-2018). These are American figures, and it is salutary that Indian literary scholars also engage with this Anglo-American tradition, instead of the French-German one which has dominated the curriculum over many decades.

item.title: Sunday book pick: Bhisham Sahni’s debut novel ‘Boyhood’ is a prelude to a pain-wracked adulthood
item.description: First published in 1967 as ‘Jharokhe’, Sahni’s novel has been translated by Anna Khanna.
item.content:encoded:
“Where does the real course of one’s life actually begin? At what turning point does one leave one’s boyhood behind and start on manhood? Who can say that, before that point, everything was clouded and unclear and without significance, but that everything ahead of it will be clear and meaningful? Isn’t manhood as hazy as childhood? And doesn’t that haziness go on right to the end of one’s life?”

Before his Partition magnum opus, Tamas, Bhisham Sahni wrote a sensitive novel about the a young boy’s coming of age in colonial India. First published in Hindi as Jharokhe (1967), it has been aptly translated into English as Boyhood (2016) by Anna Khanna. Like a jharokha balcony opening into the world, the novel opens into the endlessly confounding journey to adulthood. Sahni, who started his literary career with Boyhood, would go on to become one of India’s most important writers ever.

Looking back

The narrative voice belongs to the protagonist’s adult self, who looks back at his childhood and narrates it as he remembers it. He assumes the role of a spectator instead of the central character, as though his childhood had simply happened, many of the events beyond his comprehension and control. item.title: Video cassettes and melancholy music: Drinking in Hindi films in 1980s Shillong
item.description: The video revolution came late to Meghalaya. On the small screen, films showed us a world of heroism and love and injustice, where so much was possible.
item.content:encoded:
Everything arrived late in my hometown – the news, wrapped up in the day-old newspaper from Calcutta. The movies came even later at rickety, smoke-filled theatres.

Not that it mattered. For most of my childhood, I don’t remember going to the cinemas.

It was one of the many things one accepted as a child in the 1980s – like the pine trees growing near our home, the mists that would curl around the hills, and the pockets of time that would open up when curfew was imposed on this sleepy outpost in the Northeast.

Years ago, when the town did not have to shut down by evening, when you could be safe on its streets after dark, our parents told us how they had traipsed down with friends to watch evening shows of Bengali films in the old Kelvin cinema in Police Bazaar.

Out at night watching movies? That was not the hometown I was growing up in. A year before I was born, riots had broken out, turning the town into ghettos of us and them.

item.title: ‘Souls of Someone’: Photobook on trans women at the Koovagam festival is sensitive and full of life
item.description: Author Shino Cherian travelled to the annual 18-day Koovagam festival where trans women ‘marry’ Lord Aravan in elaborate ceremonies.
item.content:encoded:
The complexity of South Asian gender and queer expressions can’t be contained by the Anglophone queer theorisation. First, because any such exercise makes one engage with South Asia’s rich and textured myth-historical past. Second, it’s this inheritance that renders the contemporary, contextual meaning to modern-day queerness, making the latter always in conversation with its past, enabling imagination of collective queer futures.

It’s not that South Asian queerness refuses to offer a comprehensible template. It just doesn’t offer an easy one, which is why artists must invent ways to engage creatively to effectively and authentically portray queer expressions. One such work is Shino Cherian’s debut photobook Souls of Someone: Myth, Magic and Mourning in Koovagam.

“Art is born out of an ill-designed world” reads a part of the epigraph that quotes Andrei Tarkovsky in the book. Activist Grace Banu in her Foreword to the book expands on the idea, and Cherian’s desire to explore and document the Koovagam festival.

Banu writes, “The brilliance of this work lies in Shino’s willingness to ‘unbecome’ the person he thought he was. He admits to his early hesitations, the knot in his chest and the queasiness of overthinking.”

item.title: What the saga of Monsieur Mounissamy tells us about Franco-Indian identity
item.description: Pankaj Rishi Kumar’s documentary ‘To Die a Frenchman’ plunges into the hidden, intimate layers of colonial violence.
item.content:encoded:
If Gregor Samsa had been born in Pondicherry, he wouldn’t have awakened as a cockroach but as a chameleon. He would have been named accordingly, such as Jean-Grégoire Samoussapoullé, Grégoire Samikkannu, Grégorius Samassamy-Mudaliar, or, with a touch of aristocratic eccentricity, Grégoire-Marie Samassamy de Oulgaret.

Because of a colonial absurdity dating back to 1962, thousands of people find themselves in this Kafkaesque limbo, caught between two nations, two cultures, two identities, and two flags. They wake to the opening bars of La Marseillaise and go to sleep humming Jana Gana Mana. Their identity eludes both France and India, while the truly schizophrenic Franco-Pondicherrians sing neither anthem correctly. As the sun sets, they forsake both anthems for Marie, le pêcheur, an old Creole tune that drunkards sing off-key in the city’s countless bars. This timeless melody, appropriate for no nation, belongs to everyone and nowhere at once.

“My father moved with ease between the language of Molière and that of Thiruvalluvar, while my uncle knew only Tamil. The former was French, the latter Indian. This anomaly stemmed from an absurdity inherited from colonial power in 1962.”

There’s a message for the world in all this, and it better listen, because India’s education crisis is a global problem.

School students have picked up where the “cockroach movement” left off last month when nationwide youth protests that began with a satirical campaign triggered by question paper leaks and unemployment forced the Narendra Modi government to let go of its education minister whose resignation the cockroach activists had demanded.

This month, frustrated school-goers in many states have decided it is their turn to push back.

They are not asking for much, just the basics that the Indian state still fails to provide nearly 80 years after Independence.

item.title: ‘Many times, ideas from a novel leave an imprint on poems under construction’: Jeet Thayil
item.description: ‘You don’t have to step out of your house to feel dislocated. For poets, this is a useful state – it keeps the work honest,’ he added.
item.content:encoded:
Strange shadows fall on poet-novelist Jeet Thayil’s face as his photos are clicked. Stranger images appear. In one, his face looks too dark, almost invisible. He likes it the best. After all, he has negotiated many shadowy labyrinths in his life, in his work. Thayil whispers that he always feels grateful whenever poetry comes to him – considering one never knows when a verse will arrive, or if it ever will.

The conversation was to start with his latest book, The Elsewhereans: A Documentary Novel, where family history, geography, memory, and imagination come together, resisting any categorisation – and beneath it all, a peculiar longing. item.title: Upper Assam’s flood catastrophe is a direct result of river and mountain grabbing
item.description: Rampant mining and deforestation have shaken the very core of the region’s fragile ecologies.
item.content:encoded:
Since July 19, an artificial flood has wreaked havoc in four Upper Assam districts. So catastrophic has this flood been that nearly 800 villages and an area of around 1,19,000 hectares of cropland have been submerged, sheets of mud have been deposited in fields and inside people’s homes and large areas in the countryside have been turned into lakes.

More than 100 people have died and roughly seven lakh have been affected. Countless cattle have died.

The worst part of this disaster is that these are places not on the map of Assam’s annual flooding. But now, they seem to be doomed, as if a malignant wound has been created that will only spread and not heal.

For a land that is shaped and reshaped by the Brahmaputra river system and its unique fluvial dynamics, floods are not new in Assam – nor unwanted. Every monsoon, floodwaters bring alive all that was parched and dormant, replenishing the wetlands and the paddy fields, and reassuring fecundity in all living beings.

Assamese society has been traditionally a flood-dependent society, not a flood-fearing or flood-resisting one.

To make sense of the current catastrophe in Upper Assam, a historical understanding of how a natural phenomenon has become disastrous in the Brahmaputra Valley is necessary.

item.title: UK drought highlights precarious food system

Much of England is now officially in drought. Reservoir levels are being closely monitored by water companies, while farmers are reporting dry soils and poor crop conditions. Further restrictions such as grazing rules could soon come into effect.

Water is recognised as critical national infrastructure. However, drought does not only threaten our water supply. It also tests the resilience of the food system that depends on it.

For most of us, that reality becomes visible in the supermarket: standing in front of a shelf with no cucumbers, more expensive tomatoes or fewer fresh vegetables to choose from. These episodes have become increasingly familiar in recent years. We notice the empty shelves, accept the higher prices and move on.

But I keep wondering: why does this surprise so many people?

The UK carefully monitors many of the systems that underpin everyday life. We publish inflation figures every month, NHS waiting lists every week and regularly report on water reservoir levels because these indicators tell us whether essential systems are becoming stronger or weaker. They provide an early indication that intervention may be needed before problems escalate. Food, however, is different. We tend to judge the resilience of our food system only after something has gone wrong.

The sun-soaked Greek island of Corfu – as well as the Durrell family’s foibles and adventures – felt a world away from my hometown’s bleak winter and all those blister packets and doctors’ waiting rooms. I became fascinated by Durrell’s colourful childhood and his longstanding career as both an author and a naturalist. I could easily recall the story’s funniest moments and parrot the most memorable lines.

On even the hardest days, it somehow seemed to help.

India first imposed the windfall tax in July 2022 to capture extraordinary gains made by oil companies as crude prices surged. The tax was scrapped two years later and reintroduced in March after oil prices rose amid the crisis in West Asia.

The special additional excise duty, through which the windfall tax is levied, has been cut on diesel exports to Rs 24 per litre from Rs 25.5.

It is difficult to not romanticise Goa. Not the hyper-curated, exaggeratedly aestheticised party destination that lives in perpetual revelry on Instagram, or the casino capital that flashy billboards at the Dabolim airport promise, but the real deal. Small villages that awaken at daybreak. Old Portuguese houses with their red benches, often under the strict surveillance of a resident dog or two. The sound of the poder and the satisfaction of biting into the still-warm crust of a fresh poi. The energy of Mapusa market. item.title: Post July uprising, Bangladesh has rediscovered 1947 – but forgotten those uprooted by Partition
item.description: The events of 1947 are increasingly being revived as a way of reasserting Bengali Muslim political identity and creating distance from India.
item.content:encoded:
For years, August 15 in Bangladesh commemorated one event above all others: the assassination of the country’s founding president, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, and most of his family in 1975. It was observed as a day of state mourning.

It rarely evoked the day British rule over the subcontinent ended in 1947 and Bengal was bifurcated. That older date was treated as an event belonging only to India and Pakistan (which attained independence one day earlier).

Bangladesh, after all, was a nation born only in 1971, the “east wing” of Pakistan that achieved its independence after a bloody Liberation War.

But now, two years after the July uprising that brought down Sheikh Hasina’s government and turned her father Sheikh Mujib into a taboo subject, that quiet estrangement from 1947 shows signs of ending.

However, the reasons for this deserve as much scrutiny as the shift itself.

An awkward question

Bangladesh’s reluctance to dwell on Partition was never simply a matter of forgetting. It reflected a deeper discomfort about where 1947 belonged in a national story built overwhelmingly around 1971.

Not immediately referencing a place or a people, The Once and Future Riot indicates a sense of tension instead. And not just between past, present and future, but also palpably in the ability of the journalist or the graphic artist to draw their reader towards some semblance of “truth”.

Throughout his career, Sacco has been well aware of the complexity of bearing or collecting witness, including the ethical complications and subject unreliability. The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement stipulates that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all. Jerusalem went a step further, describing the alliance as an anti-Israel alliance.

But the Nato comparison is the wrong framing. Three of America’s own partners have bound themselves together – and the most consequential audience for what they signed sits not in Tehran or Tel Aviv but in Washington. The agreement reads, in effect, as a verdict on American reliability.

On paper, the combination is formidable. Turkey fields Nato’s second-largest army and a drone industry that has reshaped modern battlefields. Saudi Arabia brings the Gulf’s deepest reserves of capital. Pakistan adds a large, combat-experienced military and the Muslim world’s only nuclear arsenal. Analysts point to genuinely complementary assets here: Turkish technology which is short of markets, Pakistani manpower short of financing, Saudi wealth short of manpower.

As a safeguard measure, the government, 16 years ago, enacted a law for the mandatory use of jute sacks and bags to contain and carry 19 essential commodities, including rice, wheat and fertiliser.

The move has been largely unsuccessful, though, with plastic and synthetic fiber invasion as packaging ingredients continuing unabated. Synthetic and poly bags have caused environmental problems such as waste disposal.

Nazmul Haque, the government-appointed jute officer in the northern Sherpur district, told Mongabay that a small semi-automatic rice mill – Sakhina Rice Mill – has exclusively been using jute sacks.

Early in 1864, a young Parsi merchant from Bombay named Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata set sail for ­ England, carry­ing a set of bills of exchange backed by a consignment of Indian cotton. By the time the ship docked in Liverpool, the price of cotton had fallen so quickly that the bills became worthless. Un- expectedly forced to manage the liquidation of his ­ father’s firm, Jamsetji took time to observe the workings of the textile mills in Lancashire, the heartland of the Industrial Revolution. item.title: In Pakistan, Prisoner No 804 seems to be everywhere
item.description: By jailing former Prime Minister Imran Khan, the country’s establishment aimed to doom him to irrelevance. But he has rendered him more relevant than ever.

It wasn’t unlike a solitary vigil.

On August 1, a social media post appeared showing a woman standing outside the Karachi Press Club, holding a painted portrait of Imran Khan, bearing the words: “Imran Khan ko riha karo”, free Imran Khan, and “Hamara leader hamen wapas dedo”, give our leader back to us.

The image of her quiet defiance elided with the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s reignited street mobilisation, marking their leader’s three-year anniversary in prison.

Together, these instances illuminate a peculiar paradox: three years of incarceration instead of diminishing the former Pakistani prime minister’s symbolic appeal seem to actually have bolstered it.

Pakistan’s political playbook has long been recycled. Something drives a wedge between a political leader and the establishment. What follows is familiar: some combination of dismissal, disqualification, imprisonment or exile, with the eventual aim of irrelevance. Once enough time has passed and the political storm settles, an accommodation is usually reached.

The case of Khan somewhat unsettled the playbook. Khan’s own ascent to power was hardly predictable. item.title: What is Gen Z’s dark and nonsensical humor trying to say?
item.description: It is less about moral values but the product of a desire to engage in more authentic conversations about what they believe.
item.content:encoded:
After Luigi Mangione was arrested in December 2024 in connection with the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, the internet did what it often does: It turned something serious into a joke.

Although Mangione has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder in New York and to federal stalking charges, viral memes at the time romanticised him as a popular – and incredibly attractive – man of the people who made corporate elites within the American health insurance industry afraid.

Some of these memes adhered to conventional forms of political satire. One, for example, quoted a speech from the movie A Bug’s Life in which a villainous grasshopper argues for the need to punish the movie’s ant protagonist to keep the other ants in line. In this meme, the political point was clear: Elites preserve power by making examples of insignificant ants who dare to challenge them.

item.title: Sugarcane powers India’s rural economy but climate change is affecting yield

item.content:encoded:
Sugarcane cultivation across parts of India’s Deccan Plateau is becoming more productive. But, it is also becoming more vulnerable to climate variability, a new long-term study finds.

Sugarcane has long shaped India’s rural economy. It powers sugar mills, supports ethanol and bioenergy production, and sustains millions of farmers. But the crop is also at the centre of mounting concerns over water use, particularly in semi-arid regions facing recurrent droughts and groundwater stress.

The study analysed 22 years of sugarcane production trends across five districts in Maharashtra and Karnataka to understand how cultivation, yields and production patterns have changed under varying climatic conditions.

“We noticed that sugarcane cultivation in Maharashtra and Karnataka was increasingly being affected by climatic variability, even though it remains one of the most important economic activities across the Deccan Plateau,” says Krishna Kumar from the Department of Applied Science and Humanities at MIT-ADT University, Pune, and one of the study’s researchers.

Sugarcane production trends in India have been studied extensively at national and state levels, but long-term district-level analyses incorporating weather variability remain limited.

item.title: What decolonising economics can look like
item.description: The discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power have shaped economic development.
item.content:encoded:
Economics shapes many aspects of our daily lives, from the prices we pay to the policies governments adopt. Yet many of the ideas taught as universal principles of economics emerged from a narrow historical context and have rarely been examined through a decolonial lens.

A recently published book, Decolonizing Economics, argues that economics is long overdue for decolonisation. Its authors contend that the discipline has largely overlooked how colonialism, empire and unequal power shaped the development of modern economies and the economic theories used to explain them.

Decolonising economics means rethinking how we understand economic development and inequality. Rather than explaining prosperity through technology, markets and scientific progress, it examines how colonisation, resource extraction and exploited labour shaped today’s wealthy economies while contributing to underdevelopment elsewhere.

At its core, it’s about shifting away from an economy that benefits the elite to one that builds people’s capabilities.

As an economics professor, I’ve been restructuring my teaching based on my scholarship on critical microeconomics, critical macroeconomics and alternative ways to build the economy.

Questioning Eurocentric assumptions

India and Pakistan fought an intense four-day war in May 2025. But while the media narrative was dominated by fighter jets, drones and missiles, the most consequential contest unfolded in orbit a few hundred kilometres up.

That short war was, arguably, the first between two nuclear-armed states to be shaped decisively by the use of satellites. Few analysts acknowledged this – and the silence matters. South Asia is now sliding into a new kind of arms race with no rules to restrain it.
